HEART-RISK DECISION BENCH

Build a person. Ask Jev.

Jev is a decision model, not a chatbot: it returns a typed answer with a probability, a reason code and a confidence, and it cannot write a sentence. Below, assemble a respondent from real CDC survey answers and Jev will judge them. Every one of the 29,952 profiles you can reach was genuinely scored by Jev before this page was built, and each profile is shown next to what actually happened to the real people in the 253,680-respondent survey who matched it.

Base rate: 9.4% of those respondents had ever been told they had a heart attack or coronary heart disease. Jev was never trained on any of them.

01Build a respondent

Held fixed and shown to Jev: cholesterol checked in the last 5 years, eats fruit and vegetables daily, no heavy alcohol, has health coverage, no cost barrier to care, high school graduate, income $35-50k.

02Guess for yourself, then be scored against Jev

A random real respondent from the survey. You see exactly what Jev saw. Say whether they had heart disease, then find out, and whether Jev got it right.

Respondent

03All 5,000 people at once

Each bead is one real respondent. Fill is Jev's band; a white centre means they really did have heart disease. Switch to the truth view and the white centres are where Jev put its red and orange beads.

04What this run measured

armtrained onaccuracyAUC liftcost / 5,000per answer
Always say non/a91.0%0.500 n/an/an/a
Logistic regression248,680 labelled respondents79.1% 0.84172.894xn/a n/a
Chat LLM (deepseek-flash)nothing, written question 61.2%0.79351.87x $0.680.93s
Jev (jev-1.13.0)nothing, written question 72.2%0.7725 2.247x$0.24 0.38s

Read this table at each model's own threshold and it looks like a Jev win: Jev flags 31.5% of people, the chat LLM flags 44.9%. That is arithmetic, not skill. The real answer needs a bootstrap (2,000 resamples, in results/rigour-review.md): the chat LLM's ranking is genuinely better (AUC difference +0.021, 95% CI [+0.011, +0.032], excludes zero) but the gap is invisible at any single cut (matched-coverage precision differences of +2.8, -0.2, +0.3, +0.2 points, every CI spanning zero).

The finding that matters is calibration. Same resolution (0.0072 vs 0.0071) and utterly different reliability (0.1147 vs 0.0012): Jev's probabilities score a Brier skill of -1.32, meaning you would do better quoting the base rate on every row. The chat LLM's score +0.087. On this task the decision model's number is not a probability of disease, and the general-purpose model's is.

The decision contract matters as much as the model

Same model, same 1,000 respondents, three ways of asking. v1 describes four risk bands. v2 rewrites those bands around the observed base rate. v3 throws the bands away and asks for the probability directly.

contractwhat it asks foraccuracyAUC what actually happens
v1one of four described bands74.0% 0.786over-assigns "elevated": flags 30% of people against a 9% rate
v2bands rewritten around the base rate65.0% 0.793worse: it flags 40%. It follows the words, not the percentages
v3the probability itself, as a typed judgement42.0% 0.8059highest AUC, but every answer lands between 8% and 19%

v3's AUC is nominally the highest, but every pairwise bootstrap CI spans zero at 1,000 rows, so that ordering is not established. What is solid is the shape: v3's number is a ranking score, not a probability, since every one of its answers landed between 8% and 19%. The cut-off belongs in your code.

Created by Rubin Varghese Built with Jev (TypeSafe System One, jev-1.13.0) and deepseek-flash for the comparison arm.
Survey data: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System 2015 (cdc.gov/brfss), a US federal government work in the public domain under 17 U.S.C. § 105. Downloaded raw and derived to 253,680 complete responses; value mappings follow the official BRFSS 2015 Codebook Report.
Every profile in this page is a synthetic combination of survey answers, and each was scored by Jev in a real API call (34,877,184 input tokens, $1.46). The population figures come from the real respondents who matched each profile.
Demonstration on public survey data only. Not a medical device, not clinical advice, and not to be used to make decisions about anyone's care. Generated 20 September 2026.
